question: What does excess mean?
true_answer: The amount you agree to pay toward a claim; only paid if you actually claim. Two types: compulsory (set by insurer, based on age/experience/claim type) and voluntary (chosen by policyholder; higher voluntary excess can lower the premium).
model_answer: Excess is the amount you’ve agreed to pay towards a claim. This excess is deducted from the total cost of your claim, and you only pay it if you make a claim. There are two kinds of excesses:  - Compulsory excess: set by an insurer and can’t be changed by the policyholder. Insurers may consider factors like your age, years of driving, and the type of claim when setting this amount. - Voluntary excess: paid on top of the compulsory amount, chosen by the policyholder. You select this amount when you renew or buy car insurance, and a higher voluntary excess could mean a lower car insurance premium.  This explanation is based on the information from the policy documents provided [Source 1][Source 2].

question: What is an 'at fault' claim?
true_answer: A claim where costs (including your excess) can't be fully recovered from another driver/party. Theft, malicious damage, and fire claims always count as 'at fault' even if you weren't personally to blame.
model_answer: An 'at fault' claim is any claim where the costs (including any excess you paid) could not be recovered in full from another driver or person involved in the incident. Additionally, any theft, malicious damage, or fire claims are always treated as "at fault" claims, even if you may not be personally to blame for the incident [Source 1][Source 2].

question: Who provides windscreen cover, and what does it cost?
true_answer: Aviva uses a range of approved suppliers. With comprehensive cover: GBP 115 excess for a full windscreen replacement, GBP 10 excess for chip repairs. Not covered under Third Party, Fire and Theft. Using a non-approved repairer caps Aviva's contribution at GBP 185.
model_answer: Windscreen cover is provided through a range of suppliers used by Aviva for windscreen claims. To book a repair or replacement, you can use Aviva's approved windscreen repairers or call their claim specialists on 0345 030 6925, available 24/7.  If you have Aviva Signature motor insurance with Comprehensive cover, windscreen replacements are subject to a £115 excess, and repairs to chips are subject to a £10 excess. If you choose a glass repairer not approved by Aviva, the maximum amount Aviva will pay towards the repair or replacement is £185.  If you have Third Party, Fire and Theft cover, you will not be covered for windscreen repairs or replacements.  In summary: - Windscreen cover is provided via Aviva's approved suppliers. - Cost for replacement with Comprehensive cover: £115 excess. - Cost for chip repairs with Comprehensive cover: £10 excess. - Maximum payment if using non-approved repairers: £185. - No cover under Third Party, Fire and Theft cover.  For arranging repairs, call 0345 030 6925 or visit the approved repairers' booking site [Source 1, Source 2, Source 3, Source 4].

question: Do I need to use an approved repairer after a claim?
true_answer: Not required, but if you use a non-approved repairer, an extra GBP 200 excess applies on top of your normal excess, and no courtesy car is provided.
model_answer: You do not have to use an approved repairer after a claim, but there are benefits to doing so. Aviva has a network of approved repairers who guarantee any work done on your vehicle for three years, or as long as you insure your vehicle with them, whichever is greater. They provide a lifetime guarantee on repair quality for as long as you own your vehicle, covering bodywork repairs, paint repairs, workmanship, and parts fitted by the approved repairer.  If you decide to use a repairer that is not approved by Aviva Signature motor, an additional excess of £200 will apply on top of any other excesses under your policy. Aviva will also need to visit the repairer to inspect and authorize the repair, no courtesy car will be provided, and the quality of repair cannot be guaranteed [Source 1][Source 2].  For windscreen repairs or replacements, if you choose a glass repairer that is not approved by Aviva, the maximum amount Aviva will pay towards the repair or replacement is £185 [Source 3][Source 4].

question: What's the extra excess for young drivers?
true_answer: Drivers aged 17-20 pay an additional GBP 300 on top of standard excess for accidental damage claims; drivers 21-24 pay an extra GBP 200. This does not apply to fire or theft claims.
model_answer: The extra excess for young drivers is as follows: - Drivers aged 17-20 would pay an additional £300 on top of their standard excess in the event of an accidental damage claim. - Drivers aged 21-24 would pay an extra £200.  It is also noted that young driver excesses do not apply for fire or theft claims [Source 1][Source 2].

question: What happens to my No Claim Discount if I have two at-fault claims in one year?
true_answer: Two or more at-fault claims in a single year steps your NCD back to nil at renewal (versus a partial step-back for just one claim, if unprotected).
model_answer: If you have two or more at-fault claims in one year, your No Claim Discount (NCD) will be stepped back to nil at renewal. This means you will lose all your accumulated NCD years and start again from zero. Additionally, if you have protected your NCD, it only covers one at-fault claim per year; it does not protect against multiple claims. Therefore, two at-fault claims in one year will still result in your NCD being reduced to nil at renewal, even if you have NCD protection [Source 1][Source 2].

question: Am I covered to drive someone else's car under my policy?
true_answer: Only the vehicle policyholder (not named drivers) gets third-party-only cover to drive another car, and only if they're 25+ when the policy started/renewed, have the owner's consent, and the other car has comprehensive cover. This does not extend to loss/damage to the car being driven.
model_answer: Yes, you are covered to drive someone else's car under your policy, but with some conditions:  - If you have comprehensive insurance, you are covered with third party only insurance when driving someone else's car. This means the policy will pay compensation for injury to others or damage to other people's vehicles or property, but it will not cover loss of or damage to the car you are driving. This cover applies only to the vehicle policyholder, not to named drivers or the principal policyholder if they are not the vehicle policyholder. Also, this cover is not available on policies in the name of a business [Source 1][Source 2].  - You must be 25 or older when your motor policy started or was renewed.  - You do not need to inform the insurer before driving the other car, but you must have the car owner's consent and comprehensive cover on your own policy [Source 3][Source 4].  - Your certificate of motor insurance will confirm if you have this cover, and you can refer to your policy documents for limits and exclusions [Source 3][Source 4].  In summary, as the vehicle policyholder with comprehensive insurance, you have third party only cover to drive other cars with the owner's consent, provided you meet the age requirement and have comprehensive cover on your own policy. However, this does not cover damage to the car you are driving. Named drivers or principal policyholders who are not the vehicle policyholder do not have this cover [Source 1][Source 2][Source 3][Source 4].

question: What's the difference between a principal policyholder and a vehicle policyholder?
true_answer: The principal policyholder is who took out the policy and can assign roles. The vehicle policyholder (main driver) is who drives the car most and earns the NCD. They can be different people but must live at the same address.
model_answer: The difference between a principal policyholder and a vehicle policyholder is as follows:  - The principal policyholder is the person who entered into the contract of insurance on behalf of themselves, each vehicle policyholder, and each named driver. They are the person who took out the policy and can choose who is a vehicle policyholder and who is a named driver.  - The vehicle policyholder, also known as the main driver, is nominated by the principal policyholder as the person who drives the vehicle most often and earns the no claim discount. The vehicle policyholder does not need to be the principal policyholder but must live at the same address as them.  In summary, the principal policyholder is the policy owner who sets up the insurance contract, while the vehicle policyholder is the main driver of a specific vehicle under that policy [Source 1][Source 2].

question: Does my policy cover damage to a rental car I'm driving abroad?
true_answer: Not directly answered in this FAQ; foreign use and driving other cars are covered separately but a rental-specific scenario isn't spelled out here, so an honest answer should flag uncertainty rather than guess confidently.
model_answer: Your policy does not cover damage to a rental car you are driving abroad. The standard insurance policy provides only third party cover when driving your insured vehicle abroad, which covers legal liability to others but not loss of or damage to your own vehicle. To have cover similar to your UK comprehensive cover when driving abroad, you need to add the Foreign Use optional add-on cover. However, this cover applies to your insured vehicle and does not extend to Driving Other Cars (DOC) cover outside the UK. DOC cover, which provides third party only cover when driving someone else's car, only operates within Great Britain, Northern Ireland, the Channel Islands, and the Isle of Man, and does not extend abroad. Therefore, damage to a rental car abroad would not be covered by your policy or the Foreign Use add-on [Source 1], [Source 2], [Source 5].

question: What is the maximum age to start a new car insurance policy?
true_answer: New policies aren't offered to drivers aged 85 and over; quotes are available for ages 17 to 84.

question: How much does Motor Legal cover provide?
true_answer: Up to GBP 100,000 for lawyers' costs to pursue claims/compensation, plus a further GBP 100,000 for costs defending against prosecution, fines, or vehicle-identity-cloning disputes.
model_answer: Motor Legal cover provides up to £100,000 to pay lawyers’ costs to help you claim financial losses (such as your excess and travel expenses) or compensation for personal injury from the person who is responsible following a motor accident or incident where you are not to blame. Additionally, it provides up to £100,000 for lawyers’ costs to defend you against prosecution for a motoring offence, defend you against fines, penalties, or legal action related to your vehicle, assist if your vehicle identity is cloned, and help pursue or defend your rights in a contract dispute relating to your vehicle. There is also a 24-hour legal advice helpline for any legal matter relating to the use of your vehicle [Source 1][Source 2].

question: Can named drivers use the Driving Other Cars cover?
true_answer: No, this cover is for the vehicle policyholder only, not named drivers, and is not available on business-named policies.
model_answer: Named drivers cannot use the Driving Other Cars cover. This cover is only for the vehicle policyholder and not for named drivers. If you are a named driver, you are not covered to drive other vehicles under this provision. Additionally, if you are the principal policyholder but not the vehicle policyholder, you also will not be covered. Normally, the principal policyholder and the vehicle policyholder are the same person, but if the principal policyholder takes out insurance for someone else who becomes the vehicle policyholder, only that vehicle policyholder gets Driving Other Cars cover, not the principal policyholder. Driving Other Cars cover is also not available on policies in the name of a business [Source 1][Source 2].
